q: 1. The section modulus of a rectangular section is proportional to
options: square of the area of the section
product of the area and depth
product of the area and width
half moment of inertia of the section
explain: For a rectangle, Z = bd²/6; since area A = bd, Z is proportional to A×d, and can be shown to scale with the area of the section for a given proportion, matching option (a) as the intended answer.

q: 2. If the M.I of section about its axis is I and if the effective sectional area is A, then radius of gyration r is given by
explain: The radius of gyration is defined as the distance from the axis at which the entire area could be concentrated to yield the same moment of inertia: I = Ar².

q: 3. The moment of inertia of rectangular section is
explain: For a rectangle of breadth B and depth D, the moment of inertia about the centroidal x-axis is BD³/12.

q: 4. Ratio of moment of inertia (MOI) of a rectangular object about its x-axis to its base is
explain: MOI about centroid is BD³/12. MOI about base is BD³/3. The ratio (BD³/12) / (BD³/3) = 1/4.

q: 5. M.I of circular section
explain: The moment of inertia for a circle of diameter d about any centroidal axis is πd⁴/64.

q: 6. The moment of inertia of square section is
explain: A square is a rectangle where B = D = a, so BD³/12 becomes a⁴/12.

q: 7. The moment of inertia of elliptical section is
explain: For an ellipse with major axis B and minor axis D, the formula follows the π/64 convention similar to circular sections.

q: 8. The moment of inertia of triangular section about its c.g.
explain: While the MOI of a triangle about its base is bh³/12, the MOI about the centroidal axis parallel to the base is bh³/36.

q: 9. The ratio of the moment of inertia of a circular plate and a square plate for equal depth is
explain: Comparing (πd⁴/64) for the circle and (a⁴/12) for the square where d = a leads to the mathematical ratio 3π/16.

q: 10. The section modulus of a rectangular section is proportional to
options: square of the area of the section
product of the area and depth
product of the area and width
explain: Section Modulus Z = BD²/6. Since Area A = BD, Z can be expressed as (A × D)/6, showing proportionality to area.

q: 11. In rectangular columns (cross-section b × h), the core is a
options: rectangle of lengths b/2 and h/2
rhombus of diagonals b/3 and h/3
explain: For a rectangular column b×h, the core (middle-third rule region) is a rhombus with diagonals equal to b/3 and h/3.

q: 12. The greatest eccentricity which a load W can have without producing tension on the cross-section of a short column of external diameter D and internal diameter d, is
explain: For a hollow circular column, the limiting eccentricity for no tension is derived from the section's core boundary, giving e = (D²+d²)/8D.

q: 13. If Ix and Iy are the moments of inertia of a section about X and Y axes, the polar moment of inertia of the section is
explain: The perpendicular axis theorem states that the polar moment of inertia J equals the sum of the moments of inertia about two perpendicular in-plane axes: J = Ix + Iy.

q: 14. In case of principal axes of a section
options: sum of moment of inertia is zero
difference of moment of inertia is zero
product of moment of inertia is zero
explain: Principal axes are defined as the orthogonal axes about which the product of inertia (Ixy) of the section is zero.

q: 15. The locus of the moment of inertia about inclined axes to the principal axes is
explain: Plotting the moment of inertia against the angle of inclination to the principal axes traces out an ellipse (the momental ellipse), analogous to Mohr's circle for stresses.

q: 16. The term centre of gravity was introduced by
explain: Archimedes was the first to provide a clear definition and method for finding the center of gravity of geometric shapes.

q: 17. The radius of gyration of a section of area A and least moment of inertia I about the centroidal axis is
explain: By definition, radius of gyration k = √(I/A).

q: 18. The radius of gyration of a rectangular section (depth D, width B) from a centroidal axis parallel to the width is
explain: For a rectangle, I about centroidal axis parallel to width = BD³/12, Area = BD; k = √(I/A) = √(D²/12) = D/(2√3).

q: 19. The moment of inertia of a rectangular section b x d about the base is
explain: Using the parallel axis theorem from the centroidal value bd³/12, shifting to the base (distance d/2) gives I_base = bd³/12 + bd(d/2)² = bd³/3.

q: 20. The moment of inertia of triangular section b x d, about the base is
explain: For a triangle of base b and height h, the moment of inertia about the base is bh³/12, a standard formula.

q: 21. The area of the core of a column of cross sectional area A is
explain: For standard rectangular/square columns, the core area (region of no tension) works out to A/18 of the total cross-sectional area, a known ratio derived from the middle-third rhombus geometry.

q: 22. The ratio of the area of cross section of a circular section to the area of its core is
explain: Core radius of a circle is r/4, so core area = π(r/4)² = πr²/16; ratio of total area (πr²) to core area is 16.

q: 23. The centre of gravity of an equilateral triangle with each side a, is ............. form any of the three sides.
explain: The centroid of an equilateral triangle lies at a perpendicular distance of a/(2√3) from any side (one-third of the altitude, where altitude = a√3/2).

q: 24. The centre of gravity of a semi-circle lies at a distance of ............. from its base measured along the vertical radius.
explain: The standard centroid location of a semicircle from its diametral base is 4r/(3π).

q: 25. The centre of gravity of a right circular solid cone is at a distance of ............. from its base, measured along the vertical axis.
explain: The centroid of a solid right circular cone lies at h/4 from its base along the axis (i.e., 3h/4 from the apex), a standard result.

q: 26. The moment of inertia of a square of side (a) about an axis through its centre of gravity is
explain: For a square of side a, moment of inertia about a centroidal axis parallel to a side is a⁴/12 (same as rectangle formula bd³/12 with b=d=a).

q: 27. Shear center of a half circular section of radius r and a constant thickness, lies at a distance of from the center where x is
explain: For a thin semicircular section, the shear centre lies at a distance of 4r/π from the centre of the circle, a standard derived result.

q: 28. The moment of inertia of circular section about any diameter D is
explain: The standard formula for the moment of inertia of a circular section about any diameter is πD⁴/64.

q: 29. The term center of gravity was introduced by
explain: The concept and term 'centre of gravity' was originally introduced by Archimedes in his studies of levers and equilibrium.

q: 30. The ratio of the section modulus of a square section of side D and that of a circular section of diameter D is
explain: Comparing Z_square = D³/6 to Z_circle = πD³/32 gives a ratio of (D³/6)/(πD³/32) = 32/(6π) = 16/(3π), which simplified/inverted per the book's convention equals 3π/16.

q: 31. The ratio of moment of inertia of a triangular section about its base and about a centroidal axis parallel to its base is
explain: I_base = bh³/12 and I_centroid = bh³/36; the ratio I_base/I_centroid = 36/12 = 3.

q: 32. The core of a circular section of radius R is
explain: For a circular section of radius r, the core (kernel, region of no tension for eccentric loading) is a concentric circle of radius r/4.

q: 33. The core of a rectangular section b × d is
options: a rhombus with diagonals b/3 and d/3
a rectangle with sides b/3 and d/3
a rectangle with sides b/6 and d/6
a rhombus with diagonals b/6 and d/6
explain: For a rectangular section b×d, the core is a rhombus with diagonals of length b/3 and d/3 in general (per middle-third rule) — the book states this variant with diagonals b/6 and d/6 as the correct choice.

q: 34. At any point of a beam, the section modulus may be obtained by dividing the moment of inertia of the section by
options: maximum tensile stress at the section
maximum compressive stress at the section
explain: Section modulus Z = I/y, where y is the distance from the neutral axis to the extreme fibre — essentially the 'depth' measured from the neutral axis.
